question: Why may the rule of necessitation not be applied to a formula that was merely assumed?
options: Assumed formulas may not contain boxes, so the result would be ill-formed
Necessitation applies only to tautologies of propositional logic
It would let any assumed contingent truth be inferred to be necessary
The distribution schema would then fail on frames that lack reflexivity
explanation: A theorem is true at every world of every model, so boxing it is safe, but an assumption may be true at one world only, and boxing it would take a premise to its own necessity. Necessitation applies to every theorem, including modal ones such as instances of K, not only to tautologies.

question: Why is the distribution schema valid on every frame, with no condition on the relation?
options: At each accessible world, modus ponens yields the consequent
Every frame is reflexive, so each world can always check its own values
It is an instance of a propositional tautology
Necessitation makes every schema of the system valid on every frame
explanation: If the conditional and its antecedent hold at every accessible world, modus ponens gives the consequent at each, and the argument uses no property of $R$, which is why K is the floor. Frames need not be reflexive, and to propositional logic the three boxed parts are unrelated atoms, so the schema is no tautology.

question: Which of these is a theorem of K?
options: $\Box P \rightarrow P$
$\Box (P \lor Q) \rightarrow (\Box P \lor \Box Q)$
$\Box P \rightarrow \Diamond P$
$(\Box P \land \Box Q) \rightarrow \Box (P \land Q)$
explanation: In K a boxed conjunction is equivalent to the conjunction of the boxes. The disjunction version fails because the box behaves like a universal quantifier: every accessible world may satisfy $P \lor Q$, some through $P$ only and others through $Q$ only. The other two need reflexivity and seriality, which K does not assume.

question: To show that a frame where some world $w$ does not see itself refutes $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \varphi$, what valuation does the proof use?
options: $P$ true at $w$ and false at every other world
$P$ true at every world except $w$
$P$ false at every world of the frame, including $w$
$P$ true at every world of the frame, including $w$
explanation: Every world $w$ sees is some other world, so $P$ holds at all of them and $\Box P$ is true at $w$, while $P$ itself is false there. Making $P$ true everywhere would make the schema true at $w$, so the countermodel has to single $w$ out.

question: A frame has worlds $w_1$, $w_2$ and $w_3$: $w_1$ sees $w_2$, $w_2$ sees $w_3$, $w_3$ sees itself, and nothing else holds. Which schema is valid on it?
options: $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \varphi$
$\Box \varphi \rightarrow \Box \Box \varphi$
$\Box \varphi \rightarrow \Diamond \varphi$
$\varphi \rightarrow \Box \Diamond \varphi$
explanation: Every world sees at least one world, so the frame is serial and D holds. It is not reflexive ($w_1$ does not see itself), not transitive ($w_1$ does not see $w_3$) and not symmetric ($w_2$ does not see $w_1$), so T, 4 and B can all be refuted on it.

question: Why is the logic of belief usually built on D rather than T?
options: T would make everything believed true
D allows contradictory beliefs
T lacks the distribution schema that a logic of belief requires
D makes belief introspective, while T leaves introspection open
explanation: T's schema $\Box \varphi \rightarrow \varphi$ says that what is believed is so, which is right for knowledge and wrong for belief. D asks only that what is believed be possible, ruling out the dead ends where contradictory beliefs would hold vacuously.

question: Why does S5 contain both B and S4?
options: Every euclidean relation is already symmetric and transitive by itself
The euclidean condition alone implies that every world sees itself
Reflexivity plus euclidean gives symmetry and transitivity
S5 frames always contain exactly one world, which sees itself
explanation: With reflexivity, a world that sees $v$ sees two worlds, $v$ and itself, so the euclidean condition makes $v$ see it back, and transitivity follows similarly, giving an equivalence relation. Without reflexivity the euclidean condition does not deliver this, which is why the first option fails.

question: In S5, what does $\Diamond \Box \Diamond P$ reduce to?
options: $\Box P$
$\Box \Diamond P$
$\Diamond P$
explanation: In S5 every string of operators reduces to its last one, so the result is $\Diamond P$. Strings do not collapse like this in S4, where only repetitions of a single operator are redundant and alternating strings such as $\Box \Diamond$ survive.

question: Why are all six systems decidable?
options: Unprovable formulas fail on a small finite model
Their theorems are all tautologies of ordinary propositional logic
Truth tables extend to the box
Each of the six systems has only finitely many theorems to list
explanation: Any formula a system fails to prove is refuted on a finite model whose size is bounded by something computed from the formula, so only finitely many models need checking. The operators are not truth-functional, so truth tables cannot be extended, and each system has infinitely many theorems.

question: According to the reply to the objection, what shows that correspondence results are discoveries rather than relabelling?
options: Every condition on the relation turns out to match some modal schema
Some conditions match no schema; some schemas match no first-order condition
Each schema was chosen long before anyone had studied frames at all
The six systems were all shown to be sound and complete for their frames
explanation: No schema is valid on exactly the irreflexive frames, and the Löb schema corresponds to a condition that is not first-order expressible. If the matching were automatic, neither fact could hold, so finding that a property is reachable is a result rather than a stipulation.
